sec.title: Background
sec.p: We recently found that peritubular cells of the human testis are a dominant site of expression of the glucocorticoid receptor (GR; encoded by NR3C1). Activation of GR by dexamethasone (Dex) strongly influences the phenotype of cultured human testicular peritubular cells (HTPCs), causing massive changes of their proteome and secretome. As glucocorticoids (GC) are also known to set the internal clock of peripheral organs by regulating clock genes, we tested such an influence of Dex in HTPCs.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We performed cellular studies with HTPCs and immortalized nonhuman primate (Callithrix jacchus; Cj)‐derived peritubular cells, organotypic incubations of testicular fragments of Cj, qPCR and proteomic, as well as immunohistochemical studies.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Basal clock gene expression levels, when monitored by qPCR under standard culture conditions, showed alterations over 24 h, suggesting an endogenous circadian rhythm, especially for BMAL1. Dex (1 µM) when added to cells, caused a strong and significant increase of PER1, followed by elevations of BMAL1, and other clock genes. This action was observed as early as 4 h after the addition of Dex. Immunohistochemistry and data mining revealed GR in testicular peritubular cells and other somatic cells of Cj, in situ. We therefore performed organotypic incubations of testicular fragments of Cj (n = 3) and found that upon addition of Dex (1 µM), mRNA levels of BMAL1 and PER1 also increased in samples of two out of three animals after 6 h. Mass spectrometry did, however, not reveal significant alterations of the testicular proteome, possibly due to the short time point and/or the fact that the somatic GR‐expressing cells represent only a small portion of the testis. In support for this assumption, Dex (1 µM; 6 h) significantly increased mRNA levels of BMAL1 and PER1 in Cj‐derived immortalized testicular peritubular cells.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The results indicate that an internal clock system likely exists in peritubular cells of the testis and that Dex, via testicular GR expressed by peritubular cells and other somatic cells, is a strong regulator of this system. In a physiological situation, GC thus may be important regulators of the testicular clock, while in a situation of prolonged stress or GC‐medication, derangements in clock gene expression may result.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Little is known about the role of glucocorticoids (GC) in the regulation of the human testicular function. We recently found that human testicular peritubular cells (HTPCs) are a dominant site of expression of the glucocorticoid receptor (GR) encoded by NR3C1. 1 , 2 , 3 These cells can be isolated and studied in vitro and are an appropriate and unique cellular model for the human testis. 4

They enable us, among others, to study actions of GCand we previously found that the synthetic GC dexamethansone (Dex) has a strong influence on the phenotype of cultured HTPCs and caused drastic changes of their proteome and secretome. 1 , 2 , 3

GC are major stress signals and also act as a timing signal for peripheral circadian oscillators. 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 Via GC action, peripheral clocks in the different organs of the body are synchronized with the central clock, which resides in the hypothalamus.

The mammalian circadian clock machinery is made up of a conservative transcriptional/translational feedback loop comprising four core clock genes and proteins, which regulate daily rhythmicity within a negative feedback loop: CLOCK (circadian locomotor output cycles kaput), BMAL1 (brain and muscle ARNT‐like protein 1), PERIOD (PER1‐3), and CRYPTOCHROME (CRY1+2). 11 , 12 Herein, CLOCK and BMAL1 encode helix‐to‐helix transcription factors, which form heterodimers to drive the transcription of PER1, PER2, and PER3 together with CRY1 and CRY, 13 via binding to E‐box regulatory elements. Once these molecules are translated, they build heterodimers in the cytoplasm to interact with other proteins, and after a time lag, return into the nucleus to abolish the transcriptional activity of CLOCK/BMAL1. Moreover, these 4 core proteins are able to crosstalk with clock‐controlled output genes to adapt physiological needs in a tissue‐ and cell‐specific manner. 14 In addition, mammalian TIMELESS gene is a less‐known circadian clock element, which also interacts with CRY and PER. 15

Expression and regulation of clock genes by GC were shown to occur in cultured cells, as well. 16 Yet, whether this is the case also in isolated testicular cells and in the testis, is not well known. Evidence exists for clock gene expression in testicular Leydig cells, 17 which express the GR.

We tested whether HTPCs express clock genes and whether Dex may regulate clock genes of HTPCs. We further examined expression of GR in the testis of a nonhuman primate (NHP) species, performed organotypic incubations, complemented by studies with immortalized testicular peritubular cells, to examine whether regulation of clock genes by Dex can also occur in the testis.

sec.title: Cells
sec.p: HTPCs were obtained by the explant culture from small testicular fragments of men (29–55 years), who underwent testicular sperm extraction (TESE). Typical genetic causes for male infertility were ruled out. We followed all guidelines and legal regulations and written informed consent from all patients was obtained (Local Ethics Committee of Technical University of Munich, Faculty of Medicine; project 491/18S‐KK). The isolation and culture procedures of HTPCs, as well as an in‐depth characterization of cells were previously published. 18 , 19 The density of cells varied between 1.0–1.5 × 105 cells per 60 mm dish—depending on the duration of the cell culture experiment. When cells reached 70% confluence, experiments were started.

Generation, characterization, and culture of immortalized Callithrix jacchus (Cj) TPCs (iMKTPCs) were also described in detail previously. 20 Briefly, frozen stocks of iMKTPs were used, 2.5 × 105 cells per 60 mm dish were seeded, grown to 70% confluence and then serum starved overnight before exposure to Dex.

sec.title: Experiment 1: gene expression patterns of circadian clock genes in human testicular peritubular cells for 24 h time series
sec.p: To examine a 24 h (circadian) expression profile of clock genes, fresh Dulbeccos Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) containing 10% fetal calf serum (FCS) was added to cells from four individual donors and left overnight. On the next day, at 09:00 a.m. (Experiment time = 0 h), samples from all four individual donors were harvested at 4 h intervals for up to 24 h. To evaluate mRNA abundance of circadian clock genes, each cDNA sample at the indicated time points was run in duplicate in quantitative real‐time PCR (qPCR) measurements.

sec.title: Experiment 2: effect of dexamethasone on circadian clock gene mRNA expression in human testicular peritubular cells for 48 h
sec.p: The effect of Dex on clock gene expression was investigated in cells of three individual patients, which were also used in experiment 1. For monitoring Dex effects, medium was changed (Gibco, Paisley, UK), followed by a starvation period in the serum‐free medium (DMEM without FCS) overnight. This was done in order to synchronize the cell cycle. On the next day, at 09:00 a.m., this medium was replaced with Dex‐supplemented medium (DMEM without FCS, supplemented with 1 µM Dex dissolved in ethanol, final concentration of 0.04%). Control conditions included a solvent control (0.04% ethanol in DMEM without FCS). Cells from all three individual donors were harvested each at t = 0 (prior to 1 µM Dex treatment) and at the following time points: 4, 8, 24, 36, and 48 h after the beginning of Dex exposure. The qPCR measurements from all patients at the indicated time points were performed in duplicates.

sec.title: Experiment 3: organotypic incubations
sec.p: Common marmoset monkeys (Cj) were housed at the self‐sustaining marmoset monkey colony of the German Primate Center (Deutsches Primatenzentrum; DPZ, Göttingen). The animals used for this study were 3.5 years old males, that is, young adult, sexually mature healthy animals. 21 Testes were obtained from three animals euthanized for scientific purposes unrelated to this study or castrated for colony management purposes. Euthanasia and/or castration were performed by experienced veterinarians following all legal guidelines. All testes were washed 3× in phosphate buffered saline (PBS) supplemented with penicillin–streptomycin and the Tunica albuginea was removed. Each testis was cut to equally sized fragments (approximately 50 mg each). Each tissue fragment was incubated individually in a humidified incubator (37°C, 5% CO2 in air) in culture medium (DMEM/F12 + GlutaMAX (ThermoFisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) + 1× penicillin–streptomycin (PAN Biotech, Aidenbach, Germany) supplemented with 1 µM Dex or with ethanol (solvent control), diluted to concentration equivalent to the treatment, for 6 h (5 treated and 5 negative control fragments per incubation period). At the end of the incubation, each fragment was placed in a 2 mL tube, snap‐frozen immediately in liquid nitrogen and shipped on dry ice to Munich. For qPCR and mass spectrometry analyses, one testicular tissue fragment / animal / treatment was randomly selected, cryopulverized, equally distributed and then subjected to either qPCR studies or mass spectrometry analyses. In order to optimize qPCR measurements, an additional fragment was used, while the remaining fragments were used for experiments not related to this study.

sec.title: Experiment 4: effect of dexamethasone on BMAL1 and PER1 expression in iMKTPCs
sec.p: This experiment included three biological replicates (passages 25–27) for 6 h Dex‐treatment of iMKTPCs including corresponding controls. As described for experiment 2, medium 20 was changed followed by a starvation period. On the next day, medium was replaced with Dex‐supplemented medium (medium without FCS, supplemented with 1 µM Dex dissolved in ethanol, final concentration of 0.04%). For control purposes medium contained the solvent (0.04% ethanol in medium without FCS). After 6 h, cells from all biological replicates were harvested and processed for qPCR measurements.

sec.title: Isolation of RNA, reverse transcription (RT‐PCR) and quantitative real‐time PCR
sec.p: For qPCR studies, total RNA from cultured HTPCs, iMKTPCs, and testicular fragments was isolated using QIAGEN RNeasy Mini‐Kit (QIAGEN, Hilden, Germany) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Between 360 and 1000 ng RNA were reverse transcribed using SuperScriptTM II (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA). Adequate final dilutions corresponding to 2 ng per qPCR‐reaction were prepared and finally applied to quantitative RT‐PCR reactions using the Luna Universal qPCR Master Mix (New England Biolabs, Frankfurt am Main, Germany). Primers (see Table S1) were designed using the primer3 tool (http://primer3.wi.mit.edu; Accessed on March 2023). Runs were performed in duplicate on the LightCycler 96 System (Roche Diagnostics, Penzberg, Germany) and qPCR expression values were calculated using the ddcq method. 22 In experiment 1, the gene expression value was normalized to the mean value across all time points and to the expression of the housekeeping gene GAPDH. In experiment 2, target gene values were normalized to the first time point (t = 0) prior to the addition of 1 µM Dex. In experiments 2 and 3, results were normalized to the housekeeping gene GAPDH, in experiment 4 the housekeeping gene PPIA was shown to be the most stably expressed housekeeping gene and was therefore used for normalization.

sec.title: Proteomic analysis
sec.p: Samples from organotypic incubations were cryopulverized and processed as described. 2 Protein digestion was performed in two steps: (i) Lys C (Fujifilm Wako, Neuss, Germany) 1:100 enzyme/protein ratio, 4 h at 37°C; (ii) dilution of samples with 50 mM NH4HCO3 to 1 M urea, porcine trypsin (Promega, Madison, WI, USA), 1:50 enzyme/protein ratio, overnight at 37°C. Mass spectrometry analysis was performed similarly as already described for Dex treated HTPCs. 3 Briefly an Ultimate 3000 RSLC nano‐chromatography system connected to a Q Exactive HF‐X mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) was used. Mobile phase A was 0.1% formic acid in water and as mobile phase B 0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile was used. Peptides were separated at 250 nL/min on an EASY‐spray column (Pepmap RSLC C18, 2 µm, 75 µm × 50 cm, Thermo Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) with a two‐step gradient from 3% B to 25% B in 160 min followed by a step of 40% B for 10 min. Spectra were acquired with a top 15 data‐dependent method and analyzed using MaxQuant (V1.6.1). As sequence database, the Cj subset of the UniProt database (downloaded February 27, 2024) was used. The heatmap and volcano plots were generated in Perseus (V1.5.3.2). 23 The mass spectrometry proteomics data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium (http://proteomecentral.proteomexchange.org) via the PRIDE partner repository 24 with the dataset identifier PXD050900.

sec.title: Immunohistochemistry
sec.p: We used sections cut from blocks used in a previous study. 25 The immunohistochemical staining was performed with the same anti‐NR3C1 primary antibody (affinity‐purified, polyclonal rabbit anti‐human NR3C1; 1:500; # HPA004248 Sigma‐Aldrich, Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany), as used before. 1

sec.title: Evaluation of the experiments and statistics
sec.p: In experiment 1, a Cosinor analysis was performed for the 24 h time series in order to examine rhythmicity of core clock genes using the Cosinor Online application tool. 26 A p‐value of < 0.05 was considered to be statistically significant. The data are presented as the mean, standard error of the mean (SEM), as is depicted separately in Table S2. For statistical analysis of the two groups (EtOH control vs. Dex treatment) over 48 h in experiment 2, a two‐way ANOVA (GraphPad Prism 7.0) was performed followed by Šídák's post‐hoc test. In experiment 4, qPCR data were analyzed using one sample t‐test and depicted as mean + SEM. Differences were considered significant at p < 0.05.

sec.title: Analysis of circadian clock gene expression in human testicular peritubular cells in vitro
sec.p: Under standard culture conditions, transcripts of eight clock genes (BMAL1, PER1, PER2, PER3, CRY1, CRY2, TIMELESS, and CLOCK) could readily be determined in HTPCs at all time points maintained over a 24 h period (Figure 1). The existence of circadian rhythms was analyzed using the Cosinor online application and statistical results are summarized in Table 1 /Table S2. Most of the genes showed diurnal changes in mRNA abundance. Two of the clock genes, BMAL1 and TIMELESS, demonstrated a prominent circadian variation and were significantly expressed in a rhythmic manner over the 24 h sampling period. BMAL1 (Cosinor analysis, p = 0.04368) was the lowest at experimental time (Ex) 3.7 h, defining Bathyphase, and peaked at Ex 15.7 h, determining Acrophase. TIMELESS (Cosinor analysis, p = 0.03934) peaked at Ex 8.2 h and reached its lowest expression at Ex 20.2 h. Other clock genes (PER1, PER2, PER3, CRY1, CRY2, and CLOCK) also exhibited circadian variations but lacked statistically significant rhythmicity. Of note, although Cosinor analysis calculated no significant oscillating amplitudes for PER3, it became apparent that this expression pattern is in antiphase to BMAL1. On the other hand, TIMELESS and CLOCK expressions are suggested to oscillate in phase similar to PER1 and PER2. Hence, our experimental data support in part the existence of a functional circadian clock in HTPC in vitro. The qPCR expression patterns and rhythm characteristics of all clock genes in HTPCs are summarized in Figure 1, Table 1, and Table S2.

caption.p: mRNA expression patterns of ciclock genes in HTPCs over 24 h. Relative mRNA levels of eight clock genes expressed by HTPCs, testucaulr harvested every 4 h over the time course of 24 h under basal conditions across 8 time points at experiment time (Ex) 0 h (09:00 h), Ex 4 h (13:00 h), Ex 8 h (17:00 h), Ex 12 h (21:00 h), Ex 16 h (01:00 h), Ex 20 h (05:00 h) and Ex 24 (09:00 h). Each blue dotted data point represents the mRNA amount at the corresponding time point normalized to GAPDH expressed as the mean values of four patients (n = 4). Solid red lines represent the estimated 24 h rhythmicity calculated by Cosinor analysis.Their corresponding parameters, as well as p‐values for rhythmicity of clock genes, are depicted in Table1, while standard error of means is reported separately in Table S2. HTPC, Human testicular peritubular cell.
Rhythm parameters for eight clock gene transcripts in HTPCs calculated by Cosinor analysis.

fn.p: Note: Mesor (Midline‐estimating statistic of rhythm): rhythm‐adjusted mean of the wave, or the value around which the fitted wave oscillates. Amplitude: difference between the Mesor and the maximum height of the rhythm. Acrophase: time at which the peak or maximum amplitude of the oscillation occurs within one cycle; Bathyphase: time at which the trough of a rhythm occurs (source: http://www.tbiomed.com/content/11/1/16).

sec.title: Effect of Dex on clock gene expression pattern of human testicular peritubular cells in vitro
sec.p: We observed that clock gene expression was affected by 1 µM Dex, as compared to EtOH‐solvent control. Unlike the solvent alone (Figure 2), Dex strongly activated gene expression of BMAL1 and PER1. In detail, a statistically significant increase (more than four‐fold) was evident for the mRNA expression of BMAL1 at 8 h (p < 0.009) and to a lesser but still significant degree at 24 h (p < 0.01) post Dex treatment. Immediately after the addition of Dex, PER1 increased at 4 h by 12‐fold (p < 0.001) and reached its maximum at 8 h (p < 0.001) resulting in an 18‐fold rise. Thereafter, PER1 declined to near EtOH control levels at 36 h, while it significantly increased again at 48 h (p < 0.05; Figure 2). PER2 and PER3 transcripts exhibited a similar curve pattern between Dex and EtOH treatments up to 8 h. After 24 h, however a sharper decline for Dex than for EtOH control was observed for both genes which was still significant (p = 0.0053) for PER2 after 48 h. Unlike CRY1 mRNA expression, which did not differ between Dex and solvent controls throughout the time course, CRY2 transcripts experienced a significant surge (p = 0.002) 8 h after Dex treatment but then dropped to approximate the course of the control group. Both, CLOCK and TIMELESS, mRNAs are present throughout the experimental period but statistical analysis indicated no significant differences in Dex‐treated versus EtOH‐treated cells in these genes.

caption.p: Effect of 1 µM Dex on mRNA expression of eight circadian clock genes in HTPCs over 48 h. Analysis of the mRNA levels of eight circadian clock genes in HTPCs treated with 1 µM Dex (which remained in the culture for the study period) compared to solvent (EtOH) control. Data are mean + SEM, normalized to GAPDH and relative to 0 h (before treatment); n = 3 for each comparison, two‐way ANOVA with Sidak's post‐hoc test; *p < 0.05; **p < 0.01; ***p < 0.001. HTPC, Human testicular peritubular cell.

sec.title: Glucocorticoid receptor and clock genes in the testis in situ and in vitro, and mass spectrometry
sec.p: GR is present in NHP TPCs (Cj), in situ, as indicated by data mining and expression was confirmed by immunohistochemistry (Figures 3A and S1). Next to peritubular cells, also interstitial cells, presumably Leydig cells were positive. To examine whether Dex actions may be of systemic impact, we performed organotypic incubations of testicular fragments of Cj, challenged with Dex. We found that 1 µM Dex after 6 h increased PER1 and BMAL1 mRNA levels in 2 of the 3 animals (Figure 3B). The identity of the PCR products was confirmed upon sequencing.

caption.p: (A) Immunohistochemical detection of the glucocorticoid receptor (GR) in C. jacchus testis. In a representative testicular section, GR staining is found in peritubular cells (arrows) and various interstitial cells, presumably Leydig cells. In the negative control (Co) no signals were found. Nuclei were slightly stained with Hematoxylin. Scale bars 50 µm. (B) Effect of 1 µM Dex on BMAL1 and PER1 expression in testicular fragments of C. jacchus in organotypic incubations, after 6 h. Results of qPCR studies are shown for. Note that both clock gene transcripts in two out of three individual animals were increased upon Dex after 6 h. Data normalized to GAPDH are represented as fold change of mRNA expression compared to solvent control group set to 1 (dashed line). qPCR samples were run in duplicates. (C) Effect of 1 µM Dex on BMAL1 and PER1 expression after 6 h in immortalized peritubular cells from C. jacchus (iMKTPCs). Results of qPCR experiments are shown. Data normalized to PPIA are represented as fold change of mRNA levels compared to solvent control group. qPCR data (+ SEM) are generated from three biological replicates of iMKTPCs (passages 25–27); each replicate was pipetted in duplicates. *p < 0.05; **p < 0.01.

sec.p: Similar to experiment 2, we challenged cultured iMKTPCs from Cj with 1 µM Dex for 6 h and found that transcript levels of BMAL1 significantly, and that the levels of PER1 even highly significantly increased (Figure 3C), as compared to controls.

To search for further Dex actions, we performed an untargeted proteomic analysis on the samples from the organotypic incubations, however, we did not detect a significant effect at the cellular protein level (Figure 4).

caption.p: Heatmap (A) and volcano plot analysis (B) of proteome profiles from organotypic incubations of testicular fragments of C. jacchus, challenged with 1 µM Dex for 6 h and corresponding control samples. In the volcano plot, the permutation‐based FDR significance cutoff (P < 0.05) is depicted by the black curves. Neither hierarchical clustering, nor volcano plot analysis showed significant differences between the proteomes of treated and the corresponding controls. FDR, false discovery rate.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: Dex is frequently used in clinical practice for a number of medical conditions, yet somewhat surprisingly, possible testicular consequences of Dex treatment in man are not well known. 27 We recently provided insights in GR‐mediated, Dex‐induced changes in human testicular cells, which encompass phenotypic and proteomic changes, 1 , 2 , 3 by using a highly adequate human cellular model, HTPCs. These cells retain the great majority of their in situ characteristics 4 and allow for functional studies.

We first studied expression of eight clock genes and then tested, whether they may be expressed in a circadian pattern in HTPCs, employing qPCR. Expression was readily detected and under standard culture conditions we found that the transcript levels of BMAL1 and Timeless showed significant circadian oscillations. For BMAL1, a key element of the clock gene machinery, this is in accordance with earlier reports of cultured cells. 10 , 16 , 28 A role for TIMELESS in circadian rhythmicity remains controversial and may depend on the cellular model or tissue. 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 , 33 In HTPCs, the significant rhythmic expression suggests that TIMELESS is a clock gene of relevance. Intriguingly, BMAL1 expression fluctuated in an opposite manner compared to PER3, suggesting that both genes are relevant components in the circadian expression pattern in HTPCs.

The other clock components did not show statistically significant cyclicity in expression levels in our study, which involved four primary, patient‐derived HTPCs, that is, cells, with some degree of heterogeneity. The cells were cultured in the presence of serum, which may affect the amplitudes or rhythmic expression of some genes. In general, metabolic states, the cellular redox state may influence clock gene expression 14 , 34 and clock components may also be governed by yet other mechanisms, for example posttranslational modifications, 35 , 36 and intracellular signaling pathways. 37 These points were, however, not at the center of our work, and will require further studies.

We rather asked the question, whether Dex is able to alter clock gene expression in HTPCs. It is well known that endogenous GC, released from the adrenal gland, acts as a timing signal for many peripheral circadian oscillators. 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 In this way, peripheral clocks are synchronized with the central clock in the hypothalamus.

As the presence of serum in the culture medium, among others, may interfere with clock genes, 38 , 39 , 40 experiments aiming to examine Dex action, were performed in the absence of FCS. We found that Dex significantly elevated the transcript levels of PER1, PER2, BMAL1 and CRY2. Further PER2 levels remained elevated over 48 h over solvent controls. Changes in abundance of transcript levels of the other clock genes examined were not significantly affected.

That GC or Dex are regulators of clock genes in mouse peripheral organs and cells, e.g. primary mouse mesenchymal stem cells, mouse liver, and kidney, 41 , 42 , 43 , 44 and NIH3T3 cells, 45 as well as in cultured rat‐1 fibroblasts 46 was described. Dex also induced a rapid increase of Per1 in bronchial epithelium and in peripheral blood mononuclear cells in vitro. 47 Yet that GC or Dex alters clock gene levels in peritubular cells of the testis was not known.

We next addressed the question, whether such a regulation in isolated cells may occur also in the testis of a NHP. In testis of Cj, data mining revealed strong GR expression by somatic cells (https://apps.kaessmannlab.org/SpermEvol/, Accessed February 21, 2024) and our immunohistochemical studies supported protein expression in testicular peritubular cells. We thus performed organotypic cultures of small fragments of Cj testes in medium without FCS. The short time point (6 h) was chosen to minimize potential culture artifacts. The results of subsequent qPCR analyses of samples from two animals showed strong responses of PER1 and BMAL1, which were both elevated (2–3 times), yet in samples from a third animal no change at all was monitored.

These results imply that Dex can affect testicular clock genes in this systemic approach. Yet, as Cj is a species, in which 10–15 times higher cortisol level than in humans were described, 48 one may expect an overall down‐regulation of GR and therefore a generally blunted response. It may be possible that further, possibly stress‐related increases of cortisol in the third, non‐responsive animal, or other experimental conditions, may have downregulated the system even more.

Peritubular cells are dominant sites of GR expression in Cj testes, next to other somatic cells. These cells contribute only a small proportion of the overall testicular proteins. Bearing this in mind, it is not surprising that a proteomic analysis of potential Dex action, especially after 6 h, did not yield significant changes. If changes occurred in somatic cells, which express GR, they most likely are “diluted.”

To address this point, we studied TPCs from Cj. We previously characterized both primary and immortalized TPCs (iMKTPCs) from Cj, 20 , 25 which as we found retain the majority of the TPCs characteristics, resemble HTPCs and therefore are a highly translational model. 20 Furthermore, we found that primary TPCs respond to Dex by reduced cytokine expression, as documented earlier 2 and we now found that iMKTPCs also respond to Dex. When we added 1 µM Dex to these cells, we found that this treatment, as in organotypic incubations, significantly induced expression of BMAL1 and PER1 within 6 h. Hence, peritubular cells are involved in GC‐driven clock gene expression.

The results in HTPCs suggest rhythmically changing clock genes. Previous studies in mouse testis reported non‐rhythmical expression of clock genes, including PER1, PER2, CRY1, and NPAS2, and therefore concluded that the mouse testis lacks circadian rhythmicity. However, circadian clock genes are rhythmically expressed in extra‐testicular ducts and accessory organs of mice. 49 , 50 Since these reports appeared, evidence has accumulated indicating robust circadian clock genes and steroidogenic gene expression in mouse and goat Leydig cells. 51 , 52 , 53 A While we did not test endogenous cortisol for the ability to regulate clock genes, the clearcut actions of Dex, found in HTPCs, iMKTPCs and organotypic testes cultures, suggest a GC‐link between the central and a presumed testicular clock in primates.

Clearly, our study with human cells and NHP tissue and derived cells has additional limitations, with respect to sample size, observation time, and inter‐individual variability. Yet, in conclusion, we report that major circadian clock genes are expressed rhythmically in HTPCs. We show that Dex strongly affects key clock gene expression in HTPCs and iMKTPCs, as well as in testis tissue of an NHP. It is possible that this mode of action is involved in the manifold consequences of Dex on HTPCs, 1 , 2 , 3 which may manifest themselves later and hence may negatively influence the normal working of the male gonad. Thus, testicular consequences may occur, when Dex is used as medication and altered clock gene expression is likely a part of this.

At present time, it is not known whether, in particular, long‐term Dex medication may affect male fertility. Our results indicate that this topic has relevance for male health and therefore requires thorough investigation. The examination of the fertility status of men receiving GC‐treatment may be a first step.
